Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Ebola Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo now deadliest in country’s history At least 2,325 people have been killed, according to government data, surpassing the death toll from 2018-20 outbreak Nadeem Badshah Sun 16 Aug 2026 20.09 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 20.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is now the deadliest in the country’s history with at least 2,325 people killed, according to government data, surpassing the toll from the 2018-20 outbreak. Congo’s public health institute said on Sunday that confirmed cases had risen to 4,945, including 101 new cases detected in the previous 24 hours. West Africa’s 2014-16 Ebola outbreak resulted in 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to the World Health Organisation (WHO). What is Ebola and why is WHO treating outbreak as global health emergency? Read more On Friday the UN warned that “Ebola is winning in the Democratic Republic of the Congo” and said the epidemic was now killing one person every 30 minutes. Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have now been affected , mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported. The latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in the DRC has made this latest outbreak the fastest growing in the known history of the virus. There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current surge in cases. Thomas Parisch, a public health specialist recently deployed to DRC with Médecins Sans Frontières, said: “Normally, as an outbreak progresses, the case fatality ratio should fall as contact tracing improves and patients are identified and treated earlier. “Instead, we’re still seeing many cases detected very late, when treatment is less likely to succeed, with many identified only after they die in the community.” Uganda has reported at least 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. In May, the outbreak of the disease in the DRC and Uganda was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO. The virus is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected people and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing. According to WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle, pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckre.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, A hole in the concrete road on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge, which was hit by a Russian drone on Sunday By Ella Kipling Â and Â Jaroslav Lukiv Published 4 October 2026, 09:48 BST Updated 20 minutes ago Major bridges in Kyiv have been hit by Russian drone strikes for four consecutive days, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine's capital. Two people were injured when the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge was struck on Sunday morning for the second day in a row, while the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times earlier in the week. The latest attack came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a surprise visit to Kyiv in a show of support against Russia's continuing full-scale invasion. Russia's military said it would be intensifying strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions. It earlier said it had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops. Video footage of Sunday's strike, verified by the BBC, shows cars moving on Pivnichnyi Bridge as a drone crashes into it before exploding, creating a ball of fire. A cloud of black smoke can be seen rising above the bridge. Other videos and pictures have emerged on social media showing a gaping hole in the middle of a traffic lane on the bridge. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were injured in the latest Russian attack. He earlier said that the Pivnichnyi Bridge's roadway was hit. Kyiv's bridges across the wide Dnipro River link the western and eastern parts, and many of the capital's estimated three million residents rely heavily on the metro lines to travel across the city. The two struck bridges are still standing - but the damage and restrictions to traffic and public transport have caused gridlock in parts of the capital at times. Large numbers of commuters cross the river, especially on weekdays. Repair teams are working to fix the damage and officials say they are planning temporary pontoon bridges, ferry services and even a tunnel under the river to keep Kyiv connected. Klitschko also said a separate Russian drone strike had damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenksy said on Sunday morning Russian drones had also attacked a warehouse in the north-eastern region of Sumy, killing one person. Meanwhile, in the central city of Dnipro, six people were injured after a communications facility was struck, he said. Ukraine's Air Force said that overnight Russia had launched 135 drones, including 52 jet-powered ones. It said that 125 projectiles had been shot down. As emergency services responded to the incidents, Germany's Merz met Zelenksy in Kyiv. They laid wreaths to Ukrainian soldiers who have been killed in the war. Merz reaffirmed his country's support for Ukraine, writing on X: "Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us. "Germany's security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well." Image source, Reuters Image caption, Merz arrived in Kyiv by train Image source, Reuters Image caption, He joined Zelensky at a memorial to fallen Ukrainian soldiers Since Merz became chancellor in May 2025, Germany has become the single largest donor to Ukraine. He said the country "needs all our support in the coming weeks", adding: "If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us." Zelensky said there would be "important agreements" made between Ukraine and Germany. The Ukrainian president has made repeated appeals for Western allies to provide more military support to the country, including supplying advanced interceptors that can shoot down new jet-powered Russian drones and also ballistic missiles. The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier this week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Russian President Vladimir Putin had earlier said his military was carrying out retaliatory attacks following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities, despite the fact that it was the Kremlin that had first launched such attacks. Putin began a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. The Russian foreign ministry on Saturday repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv. Responding to the warning, EU ambassador KatarÃ­na MathernovÃ¡ wrote on X on Sunday: "The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!" German ambassador to Ukraine, Boris Ruge, reacted to Mathernova's post with: "Amen - we're staying". Image source, Reuters Image caption, In Friday's attack, a Russian drone hit cables of Kyiv's Pivdennyi bridge Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday. Klitschko warned that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities. Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable. Russia-Ukraine War Some in NATO Trying to Turn Ukraine War Into Conflict Between Alliance and Russia, Says Slovak PM NATO maintains it is a defensive alliance that operates on its deterrence and defense posture. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Slovakia's Prime Minister Robert Fico speaks at the Conservative Political Action Conference at the Gaylord National Resort & Convention Center in Oxon Hill, Md., on Feb. 21, 2025. Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo Victoria Friedman 9/21/2026 | Updated: 9/21/2026 0:00 X 1 Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said some within NATO are seeking a conflict between the alliance and Russia, after a “failed” strategy to defeat Moscow through its war with Ukraine, his comments coming as Western nations have warned that Russian hybrid attacks are intensifying. In remarks earlier last week, Fico said a drone incursion could result in the activation of NATO’s collective defense clause, Article 5, under which an armed attack against one ally is considered an attack against them all. “The failure of the strategy to destroy Russia through the war in Ukraine has ​led some Western politicians to believe that if the goal cannot be achieved through the Ukrainian army and full support for it, then every effort must be made to trigger a conflict between NATO ​and Russia,” Fico said in a video message shared on social media on Sept. 19. The war ​in Ukraine is neither NATO’s nor Slovakia’s conflict, he said, but “certain war hawks within NATO are trying, ‌at any ⁠cost, to turn this war into a conflict between Russia and NATO.” NATO maintains that it is a defensive alliance that operates on its deterrence and defense posture. According to the alliance, when Article 5 is invoked, that demonstration of this solidarity does not necessarily have to be military, and it is up to each individual ally to determine what it deems necessary in terms of support and what form that assistance takes. Related Stories Denmark Signals Trump Greenland Deal Would Boost Arctic Security Macron Calls for Plan to Protect Against Russian Hybrid Attacks Russia has also said it is not looking for conflict with NATO in Europe but will defend itself if attacked first. Hybrid Attacks Intensifying The remarks came as French President Emmanuel Macron said Russian hybrid attacks were intensifying. Hybrid attacks fall short of an act of war and can include sabotage, propaganda, and other non-overt tactics. “In recent weeks, the threat—particularly the Russian hybrid threat—facing Europeans and France has intensified,” ​Macron said in Paris on Sept. 18, saying that his administration would be drawing up plans on how to protect critical infrastructure from drone attacks. The French president cited an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August, which German authorities blamed on Russia, as evidence of Moscow’s changing demonstrations of aggression. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk on Sept. 17 cited unnamed intelligence agencies saying that Moscow is planning to launch “hybrid” drone and ​missile attacks against countries that are supporting Ukraine. “These potential strikes would be quote-unquote ‘accidental’ in nature, ‌intended to paralyze or at least weaken the resolve of NATO states to invoke the relevant NATO provisions in the event of aggression against a member country,” Tusk told Parliament. Russia has denied it was involved in the incident against the Leipzig airport and denies that its drones are intentionally entering NATO airspace. Slovak Relations With Russia Fico wrote in an X post on Sept. 20 that he is not “and will never be, among those looking for a pretext for war between NATO and Russia.” “As long as I am Prime Minister of the Slovak Republic, I will not agree to Slovak soldiers taking part in any military adventure provoked by anyone within NATO,” he said. The Slovak prime minister said that Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty provides members with “several options for demonstrating solidarity.” A member of the European Union (EU) as well as NATO, Slovakia has maintained diplomatic and economic relations with Russia. Hungary, under the premiership of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, similarly maintained a friendly relationship. During his tenure, Orban blocked EU sanctions packages against Moscow, was an opponent of Brussels’s plans to ban Russian energy imports, and made multiple trips to Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Budapest has taken a different approach since the election of Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar, reversing many of those policies and aligning itself more with the rest of the EU and NATO, including labeling Russia a “threat to the global order.” Recently, Budapest expelled 10 Russian diplomats. Exact details were not given, but Budapest said on Sept. 8 that their alleged engagement in certain activities was unacceptable under international codes of diplomatic behavior. Reuters and Guy Birchall contributed to this report. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The train completed an 860-kilometre journey from Saldanha Bay on the country's west coast to an inland iron ore mine on 18 October. The wagons were empty during the test run. Electric and diesel locomotives positioned along the train provided the power needed to move the massive convoy. Transnet says the train surpasses the previous record set in 2001 by a 4.5-mile-long freight train travelling from an iron ore mine to a port in Western Australia. https://seenandheard-international.com/2.text: United States Various: Ensemble Connect. Carnegie Hall, New York, 26.10.2026. (RP) Laurel Gagnon (violin), Joseph Vaz (piano) and Anoush Pogassian (clarinet) in Bartók’s Contrasts © Fadi Kheir Ligeti – Trio for Violin, Horn and Piano Loeffler – Two Rhapsodies for Oboe, Viola and Piano Kodály – Serenade, Op.12 Bartók – Contrasts for Violin, Clarinet and Piano, BB116 Cohesion is a given with Ensemble Connect. Its name suggests as much, as does the ensemble’s singular ability to engage an audience. But the individual virtuosity of its members made its season-opening concert particularly exciting, with works by three 20th-century titans of Hungarian music and one by an unjustly neglected American composer. György Ligeti was a defining force in postwar modern music. Having survived the Holocaust and later fleeing Hungary after the 1956 uprising, he developed a distinctive musical language that moved beyond traditional tonality and conventional forms, combining micropolyphony and rhythmic complexity with wit and surreal humor. His Trio for Violin, Horn and Piano bears the subtitle ‘Hommage à Brahms’. As hornist Will Sands explained, the tribute is more limited than the title might suggest as Ligeti disavowed any broader musical debt to Brahms. The connection is nevertheless clear in the combination of instruments, modeled on Brahms’s Horn Trio in E-flat major and his influence on Ligeti’s horn writing. The first movement featured an engaging dialogue between Sands and violinist Laurel Gagnon, whose playing combined tonal allure with wistful lyricism. Pianist Joseph Vaz propelled the aptly titled Vivacissimo molto ritmico , while Sands added aural exuberance with his horn’s bell pointed upward. In the final movement, the trio shaped a haunting landscape of shifting textures and intensifying emotion around a descending lament motif. Particularly striking was the purity of tone Gagnon and Sands brought to the exposed, sustained notes, lending the music an almost otherworldly stillness. A twist came with Charles Martin Loeffler and his Two Rhapsodies. Born in Germany, Loeffler immigrated to the United States but remained a Francophile. He served as assistant concertmaster of the Boston Symphony Orchestra for more than two decades. Though rarely programmed today, his music was highly regarded in his lifetime for its rich harmonies, impressionistic colors and evocative, often mystical moods. The Two Rhapsodies were inspired by poems by French Symbolist Maurice Rollinat, whose macabre, dreamlike imagery suited Loeffler’s sensibilities. The first, ‘L’Étang’ (The Pond), evokes an eerie, otherworldly landscape; the second, ‘La Cornemuse’ (The Bagpipe), conjures the haunting wail of bagpipes through modal melodies and open fifths. Oboist JJ Silvey read the poems in English translation before each work. In ‘L’Étang’, Vaz created shimmering pools of sound over which Silvey and violist Abby Smith exchanged lyrical phrases, casting an evocative, ambiguous spell. Silvey’s plangent tone contrasted with the depth and richness Smith drew from the viola. Vaz again established a mysterious atmosphere in ‘La Cornemuse’, where the two players created a shared soundscape rather than engaging in direct dialogue. The oboe suggested the distant wail of bagpipes, while the viola contributed a dark, plaintive color. At the close, Silvey’s subdued playing and Vaz’s delicate touch produced an ending as gorgeous as it was haunting. Zoltán Kodály (1882–1967) is arguably better known for the music education method bearing his name, which uses folk songs to teach pitch, rhythm, sight-reading and musical literacy, than for his compositions. A close friend of Béla Bartók, he pioneered the systematic study of Hungarian folk music with him. As a composer, Kodály drew on these traditions to create a melodic, folk-rooted language distinguished by adventurous harmonies. His Serenade for two violins and viola combines Hungarian folk vitality with a distinctive interplay among the three instruments. The first movement opens with a burst of rhythmic energy, followed by an eloquent melody from Smith’s viola over lively pizzicato from the violins, with Ensemble Connect alum Rubén Rengel partnering Gagnon. The slow second movement stood out for the expressive dialogue between Gagnon and Smith over the second violin’s tremolo. All three joined in the energetic folk–dance rhythms of the Vivo , with Gagnon delivering particularly fiery playing, capped by a brilliant violin flourish. Bartók was one of the most influential figures in 20th–century music, incorporating the rhythms, modes and melodic contours of Hungarian and neighboring folk traditions into his compositions. Contrasts , commissioned by jazz clarinetist Benny Goodman, is a virtuosic trio for clarinet, violin and piano that transforms the vitality and earthiness of folk idioms into sophisticated chamber music. Clarinetist Anoush Pogassian joined Gagnon and Vaz, matching the violinist in exploiting the wide range of colors Bartók created for their instruments. She impressed with her vibrant tone and stylistic versatility, moving effortlessly between jazz inflections and the slides, trills and elaborate cadenzas of Hungarian-inspired passages. In the mysterious middle movement, she and Gagnon engaged in precisely coordinated counterpoint while Vaz provided a sparse but atmospheric foundation. In the concluding Sebes (Fast Dance), Gagnon switched to a specially retuned second violin, whose harsh, raw sonority evoked a folk fiddle, while Pogassian played a different clarinet. These changes heightened the movement’s contrasts in color and character. Gagnon brought the performance to a close with a brilliant cadenza, capping a concert marked from the outset by style, energy and flair.
